Compare random-intercept inference choices

Source: vignettes/articles/random-intercept-inference.Rmd
random-intercept-inference.Rmd

The optional Gaussian random-intercept adapter separates the variance-fitting criterion from the fixed-effect interval method. criterion is either "ML" or "REML"; interval_method is either "normal" or "profile". Profile intervals are available only with ML. Every accepted fit returns point estimates for alpha, beta, sigma2 and tau2. Only the two fixed effects receive intervals, at both 90% and 95% from the same fit. Variance targets remain point-only.

Put the methods in one paired study

Install the optional lme4 package separately before fitting this model. The following example fits ML normal, REML normal and ML profile intervals on the same generated data in each replication. The four repetitions show how to call the API; they are far too few to assess calibration. The example chunk is not evaluated when the article is built.

library(groundtruth)

scenario <- gt_ri_scenario("inference-example", n_groups = 20L,
                           group_sizes = 6L, alpha = 1, beta = 0.7,
                           sigma = 1, tau = 0.5,
                           x_level = "observation")
adapters <- list(
  gt_lmm_adapter("ml-normal", criterion = "ML",
                 interval_method = "normal"),
  gt_lmm_adapter("reml-normal", criterion = "REML",
                 interval_method = "normal"),
  gt_lmm_adapter("ml-profile", criterion = "ML",
                 interval_method = "profile", profile_timeout = 60)
)
study <- gt_runstudy(scenario, adapters = adapters, reps = 4L,
                     seed = "20261017")

ml_vs_reml <- gt_compare_inference(study, "ml-normal", "reml-normal")
ml_vs_profile <- gt_compare_inference(study, "ml-normal", "ml-profile")
details <- gt_inference_details(study)
head(details)

Each comparison is a paired comparison within one study. The helper checks that each method has one target row for every matching scenario, replication, coefficient and level, and checks the planned replication schedule or attempt ledger when present. Its differences are comparison minus baseline. Review schedule_verified before interpreting the result; equal replication numbers from separate studies do not prove that the methods received the same data.

Read both coverage denominators

baseline_coverage and comparison_coverage condition on a finite usable interval from the corresponding method. The finite covered-interval yield divides the number of finite intervals containing truth by all scheduled attempts. A failed fit, missing interval, nonfinite endpoint, unbounded set or incomplete profile contributes zero when no usable finite interval is recorded. A missing companion leaves its diagnostic state unknown. Legacy intervals still contribute when their usable-interval flag is true; an unknown diagnostic state does not imply an unbounded set or a missing finite interval. Conditional coverage can therefore look high even when many attempts have no usable interval; yield retains that loss in its denominator.

coverage_difference_mcse is a paired first-order ratio/delta-method Monte Carlo standard error. finite_yield_difference_mcse is the sample standard deviation of paired covered-per-attempt indicators divided by the square root of the attempt count. These MCSEs describe asymptotic uncertainty from the finite simulation; they do not show that either interval method is calibrated. A missing coverage or MCSE means the required denominator or sample size is unavailable, not zero coverage. The optional joint width difference uses only replications with usable finite intervals under both methods and is descriptive.

gt_inference_details() gives one row per recorded coefficient interval, with the scenario, replication, adapter, target, nominal level, state, criterion, method, endpoints, root-LR residual, endpoint distance, elapsed time and message when available. The states are finite, unbounded, incomplete, error, timeout and invalid. An absent state row is unknown; it is not evidence of an unbounded interval. Only finite ordered endpoints enter the legacy usable-interval coverage denominator. A timeout or failed search is not evidence that the confidence set is unbounded. If profiling fails after the point fit was accepted, the point estimates remain available and the interval state records the failure.

How the two interval methods work

With interval_method = "normal", the adapter reconstructs the fixed-effect covariance at the selected ML or REML variance estimates as (X' V^-1 X)^-1. It uses normal quantiles at 90% and 95%, with no Student t correction and no extra residual-scale multiplier. These are approximate plug-in intervals.

With criterion = "ML" and interval_method = "profile", the adapter profiles the likelihood for each fixed effect. The endpoints use asymptotic likelihood-ratio cutoffs. ML normal and ML profile use the same point-estimation procedure; their paired comparison concerns interval construction, not two independent estimators. They do not establish small-sample coverage, and a finite profile is not guaranteed. criterion = "REML" with interval_method = "profile" is rejected. ML and REML use different objective functions, so their objective values should not be compared by magnitude.

Fit diagnostics record the objective convention. The REML negative log likelihood includes log|X' V^-1 X| in addition to the covariance determinant and residual quadratic, under the documented explicit Gaussian convention. Its magnitude cannot be ranked against the ML objective.

The hard profile deadline covers profiling after the accepted base fit. It requires POSIX process support; on unsupported platforms profiling records error states while preserving accepted point estimates. The deadline does not limit time spent in the base fit.

The design can limit information about the group variance. With two groups and a predictor constant within each group, the REML likelihood is flat in tau2 at fixed sigma2. In that case, the reported tau2 and its plug-in fixed-effect covariance depend on the arbitrary fitted value. Do not interpret this as variance recovery or require agreement between engines. This information limit is distinct from a singular tau2 = 0 fit or residual-variance collapse. Two groups, within-group replication and a full-rank fixed-effect design do not by themselves prove that both variance components are identifiable.

The reliability map describes the earlier ML normal-interval study. It does not evaluate REML or profile intervals. The comparison helper reports paired finite-sample summaries; it does not designate a calibrated method.
